claims.claim: A translation must avoid colloquialism and false modernity and be literary and traditional, because the original's diction was poetical, archaic and artificial in its own day.
The language should be intentionally antiquated but not arcane — words still in literary use among educated people — avoiding both the colloquial and the obscure.
claims.source: Philip Irving Mitchell (DBU), outline of 'On Translating Beowulf'
claims.quote: avoid both the colloquial and the obscure

claims.claim: The translator owes allegiance to the original's meaning and style and renders it into modern literary English, not present-day colloquial English.
claims.source: Tolkien Estate, J.R.R. Tolkien 'Thoughts on Translation (Beowulf)'

claims.claim: Resolving Old English compounds into phrases keeps colour but loosens and weakens the texture; compact naming is preferred.
Publishing The Hobbit under the convention that fairy-stories are for children had unfortunate effects on its mode of expression and narrative method, which he would have corrected if not rushed.
claims.source: Carpenter (ed.), The Letters of J.R.R. Tolkien, no. 215 to Walter Allen (April 1959, unsent draft)
claims.quote: unfortunate effects on the mode of expression and narrative method

claims.claim: Intelligent children of good taste single out the points in manner where the address is to children as blemishes.
claims.quote: singled out the places where the address was to children

claims.feature: whimsy to historical (register arc of The Hobbit)
claims.claim: The Hobbit begins in a whimsy, even facetious, mode and moves steadily to a more serious, consistent and historical one — and he regrets much of the early manner.
claims.source: The Letters of J.R.R. Tolkien, no. 215

claims.feature: LotR addressed to no class of reader
claims.claim: The Lord of the Rings was not specially addressed to children or any other class but to anyone who enjoys a long exciting story; adult language is assumed.
claims.source: The Letters of J.R.R. Tolkien, no. 215

claims.claim: In so far as The Hobbit was dressed up as for children in style or manner, Tolkien regrets it, and so, he says, do the children.
claims.source: The Letters of J.R.R. Tolkien, no. 165 to Houghton Mifflin (June 1955)
claims.quote: in style or manner, I regret it

claims.claim: Words like plenilune and argent are beautiful before they are understood; limiting vocabulary to a child's supposed reach cuts off the gifted from extending it.
claims.source: The Letters of J.R.R. Tolkien, no. 234 to Jane Neave (22 Nov 1961)
claims.quote: beautiful words before they are understood

claims.feature: first meeting in a living context
claims.claim: A fine word should first be met in a living context, not a dictionary; 'argent' does not mean 'silver' because its phonetic incarnation and heraldic overtones differ.
claims.source: The Letters of J.R.R. Tolkien, no. 234
claims.quote: in a living context, and not in a dictionary

claims.claim: Tolkien deprecated the writing-down, flattening attitude that leaves children with little respect and no love for words; The Hobbit's early part was his one such mistake.
The Lord of the Rings is meant to include, even in style, the colloquialism and vulgarity of hobbits, poetry, and the highest style of prose.
claims.source: The Letters of J.R.R. Tolkien, no. 131 to Milton Waldman (1951)
claims.quote: the colloquialism and vulgarity of Hobbits

claims.feature: tone rises with the hero's development
claims.claim: In The Hobbit the tone and style change with the hobbit's development, passing from fairy-tale to the noble and high and relapsing on the return.
claims.source: The Letters of J.R.R. Tolkien, no. 131
claims.quote: passing from fairy-tale to the noble and high

claims.claim: The legendarium ranges from the cosmogonic to the fairy-story level, the larger founded on the lesser and the lesser drawing splendour from the vast backcloths.
claims.source: Wikipedia, 'Impression of depth in The Lord of the Rings' (citing Letter 131)
claims.quote: the lesser drawing splendour from the vast backcloths

verdicts.trueWording: avoid 'colloquialism and false modernity'; 'literary and traditional'
verdicts.note: Raw en.wikipedia.org/wiki/On_Translating_Beowulf fetched by curl (200). Quote 'colloquialism and false modernity' appears verbatim (Magennis quoting Tolkien). Every limb supported: the same block carries "your language must be literary and traditional: not because it is now a long while since the poem was made ... but because the diction of Beowulf was poetical, archaic, artificial (if you will), in the day that the poem was made."

verdicts.trueWording: antiquated not arcane; avoid the colloquial and the obscure
verdicts.unsupportedLimb: 'words still in literary use among educated people' — that qualifier appears nowhere on the DBU page (full page text read, 6,116 chars; no occurrence of 'educated' or 'literary use')
verdicts.note: Raw dbu.edu page fetched by curl (200). Quote 'avoid both the colloquial and the obscure' is verbatim, and 'intentionally antiquated but not intentionally arcane' supports that limb; the 'still in literary use among educated people' gloss is imported from Tolkien's essay, not from this page.

verdicts.trueWording: 'absolute allegiance to the thing translated: to its meaning, its style'
verdicts.note: Raw tolkienestate.com page fetched by curl (200). Quote 'modern literary, not present-day colloquial' verbatim, in the parenthesis '(modern literary, not present-day colloquial) English is an instrument of very great capacity'. Allegiance limb verbatim too: 'First of all by absolute allegiance to the thing translated: to its meaning, its style, technique, and form.'

verdicts.trueWording: 'Choice between the evils will vary with occasions'
verdicts.unsupportedLimb: 'compact naming is preferred' — the page states no preference; it says the naming method 'retains the compactness of the original but loses its colour' and closes 'Choice between the evils will vary with occasions'
verdicts.note: Raw Wikipedia page fetched by curl (200). Quote 'loosens and weakens the texture' verbatim, and the colour/texture trade-off is exactly as claimed; but the page presents the two methods as balanced evils rather than favouring compact naming.

verdicts.trueWording: 'if I had not been rushed, I should have corrected'
verdicts.note: Letters PDF fetched (200, 1.88 MB, 493 pp) and text-extracted with pypdf. Letter 215 To Walter Allen, unsent draft (PDF p.309): 'When I published The Hobbit – hurriedly and without due consideration – I was still influenced by the convention that fairy-stories are naturally directed to children ... But it had some unfortunate effects on the mode of expression and narrative method, which if I had not been rushed, I should have corrected.' Quote verbatim; all limbs supported.

verdicts.trueWording: 'Intelligent children ... singled out the places where the address was to children as blemishes'
verdicts.unsupportedLimb: 'of good taste' — the Tolkien Gateway page says only 'Intelligent children, he was glad to say'; the qualifier is absent from this page
verdicts.note: tolkiengateway.net returns 403 behind a Cloudflare 'Just a moment...' challenge to curl with both Chrome and Safari UAs plus full navigation headers; recovered via Wayback raw capture https://web.archive.org/web/20260104191641id_/https://tolkiengateway.net/wiki/Letter_215 (200). Quote is verbatim there. The 'of good taste' limb IS in the primary text (Letters PDF, Letter 215: 'Intelligent children of good taste (of which there seem quite a number)') but not on the cited page, so the claim is sound and the citation is short of it.

verdicts.trueWording: begins 'whimsy', even facetious; moves to serious/historical; 'I regret much'
verdicts.note: Letters PDF, Letter 215 (PDF pp.309-310): 'The Hobbit can be seen to begin in what might be called a more "whimsy" mode, and in places even more facetious, and move steadily to a more serious or significant, and more consistent and historical. .... But I regret much of it all the same.' Quote 'more consistent and historical' verbatim; every limb supported (page reads 'more serious or significant' where the claim says 'more serious').

verdicts.trueWording: 'not specially addressed to children or to any other class of people'
verdicts.note: Letters PDF, Letter 215: 'that work was not specially addressed to children or to any other class of people. But to any one who enjoyed a long exciting story, of the sort that I myself naturally enjoy.' Quote verbatim. Adult-language limb supported in the same letter: 'I am not specially interested in children, and certainly not in writing for them: i.e. in addressing directly and expressly those who cannot understand adult language.'

verdicts.trueWording: 'In so far as it was dressed up as "for children" ... I regret it. So do the children.'
verdicts.note: Letters PDF at Letter 165 To the Houghton Mifflin Co. (PDF p.232). Quote 'in style or manner, I regret it' verbatim, and 'So do the children' immediately follows; the editorial bracket '[The Hobbit]' fixes the referent. Location caveat: the sentence sits in Carpenter's headnote to Letter 165, quoting Harvey Breit's 5 June 1955 New York Times column drawn from Tolkien's own answers, not in the body of the 30 June 1955 letter — which opens 'Please do not blame me for what Breit made of my letter!'

verdicts.trueWording: 'you ... simply cut off the gifted ones from the chance of extending it'
verdicts.note: Letters PDF, Letter 234 To Jane Neave, 22 November 1961 (PDF p.330): 'As for plenilune and argent, they are beautiful words before they are understood'. Quote verbatim; second limb verbatim too: 'As soon as you limit your vocabulary to what you suppose to be within their reach, you in fact simply cut off the gifted ones from the chance of extending it.'

verdicts.trueWording: 'They think argent "means" silver. But it does not.'
verdicts.note: Letters PDF, Letter 234: 'surely the first meeting should be in a living context, and not in a dictionary, like dried flowers in a hortus siccus!' Quote verbatim. Both remaining limbs on the page: 'clothed in a totally different phonetic incarnation' and 'the heraldic overtones it has ... which "silver" has not'.

verdicts.trueWording: deprecated it; 'only made the mistake once, in the early part of The Hobbit'
verdicts.note: tolkiengateway.net 403 (Cloudflare challenge) on the live URL with browser UAs; recovered via Wayback raw capture https://web.archive.org/web/20260107071600id_/https://tolkiengateway.net/wiki/Letter_234 (200). Page: 'Tolkien deprecated the writing down, flattening attitude that made so many children have little respect and no love for words.' Quote verbatim; the one-mistake limb is supported earlier on the same page: 'He had only made the mistake once, in the early part of The Hobbit.'

verdicts.trueWording: 'even in style it is to include the colloquialism and vulgarity of Hobbits'
verdicts.note: Letters PDF, Letter 131 To Milton Waldman (PDF p.167 header; passage at p.177): '...even in style it is to include the colloquialism and vulgarity of Hobbits, poetry and the highest style of prose.' Quote verbatim (pypdf inserts stray intra-word spaces such as 'styl e' / 'colloquialis m'; the whitespace-stripped text matches the quote exactly).

verdicts.trueWording: 'relapsing with the return' (claim says 'on the return')
verdicts.note: Letters PDF, Letter 131: 'as a critic has perceived) the tone and style change with the Hobbit's development, passing from fairy-tale to the noble and high and relapsing with the return.' Quote verbatim; all limbs supported, the only difference being the preposition ('with the return' vs the claim's 'on the return').

verdicts.trueWording: 'the larger founded on the lesser in contact with the earth'
verdicts.note: Raw en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Impression_of_depth_in_The_Lord_of_the_Rings fetched by curl (200). Blockquote: 'ranging from the large and cosmogonic, to the level of romantic fairy-story—the larger founded on the lesser in contact with the earth, the lesser drawing splendour from the vast backcloths'. Quote verbatim; the page's reference list confirms the source as 'Carpenter 2023, Letter #131 to Milton Waldman, late in 1951'.
